repos.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
repos.paper_summary:
AutoGen is an open-source framework for building LLM applications via multi-agent conversations. The system defines two core concepts: conversable agents, which are customizable entities backed by LLMs, tools, or human inputs, and conversation programming, a method that structures application logic around inter-agent message passing and control flow. Agents use unified interfaces to send messages and generate replies, with an auto-reply mechanism driving the workflow without a central controller. Developers can program interaction patterns using Python code or natural language instructions embedded in agent prompts.

The paper evaluates AutoGen across six domains. On the MATH dataset (5000 problems), the default two-agent configuration achieved 69.48% accuracy, outperforming vanilla GPT-4 at 55.18%. In ALFWorld decision-making tasks, adding a "grounding" agent improved performance by 15% over a ReAct baseline. For coding tasks on OptiGuide, a multi-agent design increased the F-1 score for identifying unsafe code by 8% with GPT-4 and 35% with GPT-3.5-turbo compared to a single-agent setup. The framework reduced the core workflow code for one application from 430 lines to 100 lines. Limitations include the reliance on proprietary models like GPT-4 for peak performance and the lack of formal safety guarantees for fully autonomous agent interactions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-agent conversation is proposed as the basis for building LLM applications, implemented in the AutoGen framework.

digest_headlines.heading: The AutoGen Framework
digest_headlines.headline: AutoGen rests on conversable agents and conversation programming, where agents exchange messages and control flow emerges from those conversations.

digest_headlines.heading: Applications of AutoGen
digest_headlines.headline: Six example applications test AutoGen across math, retrieval, decision making, coding, group chat and chess.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The discussion frames AutoGen as a general framework and states that its experiments are early, with safety questions left open.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics statement
digest_headlines.headline: The ethics statement names privacy, bias, accountability, trust and unintended consequences as risks to address.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work with a comparison table, expanded discussion, usage guidelines, future work, and supporting figures.

repos.title: One Token Is Enough: Fingerprinting and Verifying Large Language Models from Single-Token Output Distributions
repos.paper_summary: The paper proposes a black-box fingerprint for LLMs: the empirical distribution of single-token answers to trivial prompts such as "name a random number between 1 and 100," sampled at temperature 1.0 in four languages with reasoning disabled and a 16-token cap. Across 165 models served through OpenRouter, the median cell entropy is 1.00 bit. The median Jensen–Shannon divergence between split halves of one model is 0.075, versus 0.489 between different models. Leave-one-out nearest-neighbour classification assigns a model to its documented family with 59.5% accuracy, against an 18.4% chance rate. A verification test gives a 7.3% equal error rate with all 40 cells and 10.6% with eight cells; a 16-cell audit uses 240 single-token queries. Verifying against a reference from a different provider gives AUC 0.880, versus 0.971 for the same provider. Limitations: fingerprints drift with model updates, multi-month drift was not measured, paraphrase invariance is left to future work, the census covers one aggregator, and endpoints with hidden reasoning were excluded. One endpoint marketed as proprietary lies at distance 0.141 from an open-weight Qwen model.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Served LLMs often differ from advertised models, so clients need a cheap, text-only identity check.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior attribution work needs long outputs, logits, or owner cooperation; this study uses one-token answers.

digest_headlines.heading: Threat Model
digest_headlines.headline: The verifier sees only text and a trusted reference, facing adversaries that substitute, filter, or emulate.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each model is fingerprinted by answer distributions over ten tasks in four languages, compared with Jensen–Shannon divergence.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The census covers 165 models from 342 catalog entries, 326,047 responses, and a total cost of USD 34.44.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Fingerprints separate models and recover lineage at 59.5% accuracy against 18.4% chance, with 7.3% equal error rate verification.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Cross-provider shifts stay below impostor distances, and no response-caching signature appears in the census.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics and Responsible Disclosure
digest_headlines.headline: Anomalies are framed as statistical deviations with benign explanations, and no security exploit is involved.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Single-token audits are a near-zero-cost check, with longitudinal drift and watermark-aware variants left to future work.

repos.title: Scientific Agent Skills: A Library of Procedural Knowledge for Research Agents
repos.paper_summary: Scientific Agent Skills is an open library of 163 procedural skills for research agents, spanning 16 areas including genomics, cheminformatics, medical imaging, study design and scientific communication. Each skill is a directory built around a versioned Markdown instruction file, often with reference documents and scripts. An agent loads the file only when a task calls for it. The paper is a resource description. It reports no task-level evaluation and no host selection rate. It measures two corpus properties at tag v2.65.0. The always-resident descriptions of all skills cost 7.1% of a 200,000-token window. The median of the 46 documented workflows fits within 23.9% of that window, although 29 of the 46 would overflow if every reference file were loaded. Lexical analysis finds a median nearest-neighbour cosine similarity of 0.15 between descriptions, with the closest pair at 0.40. Limitations include no evidence that skills improve agent outcomes, no measured selection accuracy, and uneven review, since 32 of 163 skills do not list the maintainers as author.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Agents often return working code that is not defensible, so the paper proposes a library of field-specific procedures packaged as agent skills.

digest_headlines.heading: What an agent skill is
digest_headlines.headline: Each skill is a directory whose instruction file is read only when relevant, keeping most documentation out of standing context.

digest_headlines.heading: What the library covers
digest_headlines.headline: The library's 163 skills cover 16 self-assigned categories, most shipping reference documents, and the workflows combine them unevenly.

digest_headlines.heading: Can descriptions distinguish among skills?
digest_headlines.headline: Most skill descriptions are lexically well separated, but a few neighbouring pairs remain close and some lack authored guidance.

digest_headlines.heading: Do the skills a workflow needs fit in context?
digest_headlines.headline: Documented workflows fit a 200,000-token window in their instruction files, but 29 of 46 overflow if every reference file loads.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The paper reports no task-level evaluation, measures selection only as a lexical proxy, and does not test host portability.

digest_headlines.heading: Availability and citation
digest_headlines.headline: Work using the library should cite the paper and tag v2.65.0, and name each skill's metadata version.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendices list the tokenizer and token ledger, skill contents, category counts, routing sensitivity and installed-base estimate.

repos.title: DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring
repos.paper_summary: DeepTutor is an open-source agentic tutoring framework that combines citation-grounded problem tutoring with difficulty-calibrated question generation, both driven by a shared learner model. Its Hybrid Personalization Engine pairs Static Knowledge Grounding (knowledge-graph traversal plus dense search, fused by reciprocal rank fusion) with Dynamic Personal Memory, a trace forest of past interactions. Three memory agents query this forest and update a learner profile after each session. Tutoring proceeds through investigation, guided solving, and evidence-based writing. Question generation selects ideas, then a separate validator checks each question, answer, and explanation. TutorBench covers five university-level disciplines, with learner profiles tied to course material and evaluated by an LLM student simulator and rubric-based assessors. DeepTutor improves personalized metrics by 10.8% on average, and a solver-only transfer study shows a 29.4% average gain across five backbone models. Human raters and the LLM judge show aligned preference trends. Stated limitations include simulated rather than real learners, no large-scale human student study, and added inference cost. The Book Engine and Partners are described architecturally without learner-outcome evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing tutoring and question-generation workflows run in isolation, so tutoring traces do not shape later practice items.

digest_headlines.heading: DeepTutor Framework
digest_headlines.headline: A shared personalization engine feeds problem tutoring and question generation, and every completed interaction updates the learner profile.

digest_headlines.heading: Extending the Personalization Substrate
digest_headlines.headline: Extensions such as Deep Research, Mastery Path and the Book Engine reuse one personalization substrate, while quantitative evaluation covers only the tutoring core.

digest_headlines.heading: TutorBench
digest_headlines.headline: TutorBench pairs 90 learner profiles from 30 knowledge bases in five disciplines with 270 source-grounded interactive tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: DeepTutor reaches 3.91 overall quality on TutorBench against 3.53 for the Naive Tutor baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers LLM memory, knowledge tracing and LLM tutors, and finds adaptive tutoring on individualized materials underexplored.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DeepTutor improves overall quality by 10.8% on TutorBench and yields a 29.4% average gain across five backbone families.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Interactive results rest on LLM simulators and rubric judges, and the extensions' effects on real learners remain untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extended related work, implementation details, TutorBench construction, evaluation protocol, hyperparameters and backbone models.

repos.title: Segment Anything
repos.paper_summary:
The Segment Anything project introduces SAM, a promptable segmentation model, and SA-1B, a dataset of 1.1 billion masks on 11 million images. SAM uses an MAE-pretrained ViT-H image encoder, a flexible prompt encoder for points, boxes, or text, and a lightweight mask decoder that predicts three candidate masks per prompt to handle ambiguity. The authors trained the model using a data engine that iterated between assisted manual annotation and fully automatic mask generation via a $32 \times 32$ point grid.

In zero-shot evaluations across 23 datasets, SAM outperforms the RITM baseline on 16 datasets with a single foreground point, achieving up to 47 higher IoU. Human raters score SAM’s masks between 7 and 9 out of 10, consistently higher than baselines. On BSDS500 edge detection, SAM achieves an ODS of 0.768 and AP of 0.794 without task-specific training. For object proposals on LVIS v1, SAM reaches a mask AR@1000 of 59.3, surpassing the ViTDet-H detector on medium, large, rare, and common objects. In instance segmentation, SAM yields a mask AP of 46.5 on COCO and 44.7 on LVIS when prompted with ViTDet boxes, trailing the fully supervised ViTDet-H (51.0 and 46.6). Limitations include missing fine structures and hallucinating small disconnected components.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The paper builds a promptable segmentation task, the SAM model, and a data engine that produced SA-1B with over 1B masks.

digest_headlines.heading: Segment Anything Task
digest_headlines.headline: Promptable segmentation asks for a valid mask from any prompt, and the same task serves as pre-training and zero-shot transfer.

digest_headlines.heading: Segment Anything Model
digest_headlines.headline: SAM pairs a pre-trained image encoder with a fast prompt encoder and mask decoder that predicts 3 masks per prompt.

digest_headlines.heading: Segment Anything Data Engine
digest_headlines.headline: A three-stage data engine moves from annotator-assisted labeling to fully automatic mask generation over all 11M images.

digest_headlines.heading: Segment Anything Dataset
digest_headlines.headline: SA-1B contains 1.1B masks, 99.1% generated automatically, and 94% of sampled automatic masks exceed 90% intersection-over-union with corrected versions.

digest_headlines.heading: Segment Anything RAI Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: SAM performs similarly across perceived gender and skin tone groups, while the older age group scores highest with a wide confidence interval.

digest_headlines.heading: Zero-Shot Transfer Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: With one point, SAM beats the strongest interactive baseline on 16 of 23 datasets and receives higher human quality ratings.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors argue SAM's capabilities come mostly from supervised training, and list missed fine structures and limited text-to-mask reliability as limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists architecture, training, automatic mask generation, fairness, study design, model and dataset cards, and annotation guidelines.

repos.title: Codebase-Memory: Tree-Sitter-Based Knowledge Graphs for LLM Code Exploration via MCP
repos.paper_summary:
Codebase-Memory is an open-source system that constructs a Tree-Sitter-based knowledge graph to expose structural code queries to LLM agents via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The pipeline parses 66 languages, resolves calls using a six-strategy cascade, and detects communities with the Louvain algorithm. It stores the resulting graph in SQLite and exposes 14 typed query tools through a single statically linked C binary with zero runtime dependencies.

Evaluated across 31 real-world repositories, the MCP Agent achieved an 83% answer quality score compared to 92% for a file-exploration agent, while consuming ten times fewer tokens ($\sim$1,000 vs. $\sim$10,000) and requiring 2.1 times fewer tool calls. Query latency was under 1 ms for the MCP agent versus 10–30 s for the explorer. Limitations include reduced accuracy on macro-heavy C code (58% quality) and the absence of source-level context, which requires fallback to file exploration for exhaustive pattern matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Text-based code exploration by coding agents scales poorly, so the paper proposes a queryable code knowledge graph exposed via MCP.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work builds heavyweight code graphs or improves agent strategy, leaving the retrieval layer largely unchanged.

digest_headlines.heading: System Design
digest_headlines.headline: Codebase-Memory parses 66 languages into one SQLite knowledge graph and serves it through 14 MCP tools.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On 31 languages the MCP agent scored 0.83 against 0.92 for the explorer while using 2.1 times fewer tool calls.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Structure helps cross-file queries, but results come from one backend and one repository per language.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues structural retrieval is a viable foundation for LLM-based code intelligence.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Availability Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The source code, benchmark scripts and evaluation data are public for the evaluated release v0.5.5.

repos.title: Gradio: Hassle-Free Sharing and Testing of ML Models in the Wild
repos.paper_summary:
Gradio is an open-source Python package that generates a web-based interface for machine learning models, allowing non-technical users to test them via a shared URL. The system supports inputs and outputs for images, text, and audio, and is compatible with Scikit-Learn, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or arbitrary Python functions. When a researcher launches the interface, Gradio creates an SSH tunnel to host the model on the original machine, enabling remote collaborators to access it through a browser without installing software. Users can manipulate inputs, such as cropping or occluding image regions, and flag incorrect predictions to send feedback directly to the developer.

The authors validated the tool in a pilot study involving an ML researcher and a cardiologist classifying echocardiograms for pacemaker presence. The underlying model achieved an AUC of 0.93. Setup took approximately 10 minutes. During testing, the cardiologist successfully identified model failures by flipping images vertically and used the built-in tools to verify predictions by occluding the pacemaker. Limitations include the study's small scope of one user pair over a short period, and the absence of quantitative measures for trust or satisfaction.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Domain experts usually cannot try ML models during development, so the authors built Gradio, a Python package that generates web interfaces.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Interviews with 12 ML researchers yielded four design requirements for interfaces, sharing, input manipulation, and notebook embedding.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: Gradio wraps a trained model in an Interface object with four required parameters and shares it through a secure tunnel.

digest_headlines.heading: Pilot Study: Echocardiogram Classification
digest_headlines.headline: A single pilot pair found the shared link let a cardiologist probe a pacemaker classifier and flag failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion & Next Steps
digest_headlines.headline: The authors expect the package to widen domain expert access, but a single short pair study cannot establish usefulness.

repos.title: LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation
repos.paper_summary:
LightRAG is a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation system. An LLM extracts entities and relations from chunks of size 1200, profiles each as a key-value pair, and deduplicates the resulting graph. At query time, local keywords match entities and global keywords match relations, and one-hop neighbors of the matches are added as context for a general LLM. New documents are indexed by merging their subgraphs into the existing graph instead of rebuilding it.

The evaluation uses four UltraDomain datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, Mix), with 125 generated questions per dataset, GPT-4o-mini as the default LLM, and pairwise LLM judgments reported as win rates. Against NaiveRAG on Legal, LightRAG wins 84.8% overall. Against GraphRAG, the margins are small: overall win rates of 54.8% on Agriculture, 52.0% on CS, 52.8% on Legal, and 49.6% on Mix.

The judgments come from a single LLM judge, not human or ground-truth labels. The ablation and cost results are cut off in the provided text, so this summary does not report them.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems rely on flat representations and produce fragmented answers, so the paper proposes graph-based indexing with incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
digest_headlines.headline: The paper formalizes RAG as indexing and retrieval followed by generation, and sets three design goals for an efficient system.

digest_headlines.heading: The LightRAG Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG builds a knowledge graph with LLM extraction, updates it incrementally, and retrieves through dual-level keyword matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG wins LLM-judged comparisons against four baselines on UltraDomain datasets, and uses far fewer retrieval tokens than GraphRAG.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work finds graph-based RAG lacks dynamic updates, and surveys three ways LLMs are combined with graph data.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG is concluded to improve retrieval speed and quality and cut LLM inference costs through graph indexing and incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, a case study against NaiveRAG, and the prompts for graph generation, query generation, keyword extraction and evaluation.

repos.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
repos.paper_summary: The Switch Transformer replaces the standard feed-forward layer in Transformers with a sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) module that routes each token to a single expert, reducing communication overhead and improving training stability. By using top-1 routing instead of top-k, the model maintains constant computational cost per token while scaling parameter count. The paper introduces selective precision casting to stabilize bfloat16 training and an auxiliary load-balancing loss to ensure uniform expert usage. Experiments on the C4 corpus show that a 64-expert Switch-Base model achieves the same pre-training quality as T5-Base in one-seventh the time. Fine-tuning results indicate consistent improvements over T5-Base and T5-Large on GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, and summarization tasks. Distilling these sparse models into dense T5-Base architectures preserves approximately 30% of the quality gain while compressing model size by up to 99%. In multilingual settings across 101 languages, the method yields a mean 5x speedup over mT5-Base. A limitation is that distillation does not fully recover teacher performance, and the approach relies on specific hardware parallelism strategies for trillion-parameter scales.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse expert routing is proposed to add parameters without raising per-example compute, with gains across pre-training, fine-tuning and multilingual training.

digest_headlines.heading: Switch Transformer
digest_headlines.headline: Routing each token to one expert simplifies Mixture of Experts, with capacity limits and a balancing loss keeping training stable.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Properties
digest_headlines.headline: Increasing experts at fixed FLOPS per token speeds up pre-training, with Switch-Base 64 reaching T5-Base quality in one-seventh the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Downstream Results
digest_headlines.headline: Switch models improve most T5 fine-tuning tasks, distill to dense models keeping 30% of gains, and beat mT5 on all 101 languages.

digest_headlines.heading: Designing Models with Data, Model, and Expert-Parallelism
digest_headlines.headline: Data, model and expert parallelism combine to train 395 billion and 1.6 trillion parameter Switch models, with Switch-XXL sometimes unstable.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work scales models through model parallelism and conditional computation, including mixture of experts and attention sparsity.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse models are argued to outperform dense models per step and on wall clock time, but distilled versions keep only about 30% of gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Remaining challenges include stabilizing the largest models, heterogeneous experts, expert layers beyond feed-forward layers, and other modalities.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Switch Transformers are presented as stable, sample-efficient language learners across pre-training, fine-tuning and multi-task training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers attention Switch layers, token rerouting, router exploration, small-scale results, upstream-downstream correlation and pseudocode.

repos.title: Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs
repos.paper_summary: Faiss is an open-source library that accelerates similarity search on GPUs by implementing a register-based $k$-selection algorithm, WarpSelect, and optimized layouts for brute-force and product quantization (PQ) based searches. WarpSelect maintains intermediate state entirely in GPU registers to avoid memory bottlenecks, using odd-size sorting networks to merge per-lane queues with a shared warp queue. This design achieves up to 55% of theoretical peak performance and makes nearest neighbor search 8.5 times faster than prior GPU implementations. The library applies these kernels to exact brute-force search, IVFADC approximate search, and compressed-domain PQ search. On the Yfcc100M dataset, it constructs a high-accuracy $k$-NN graph over 95 million images in 35 minutes. It builds a graph connecting 1 billion vectors in under 12 hours using four Maxwell Titan X GPUs. The implementation supports vector dimensions up to 64 sub-vectors for PQ codes. Limitations include reliance on specific NVIDIA hardware features like warp shuffles and a requirement that input data fits within the GPU’s global memory or be streamed efficiently from host memory.
